passage: Four boys in one neighbourhood were each dared to do something risky that summer. Rishi stood on top of a high wall while the others jeered, "Jump, jump!" He pictured a broken leg on one side and a few minutes of teasing on the other. Jokes fade quickly, he decided, but a leg takes long to mend, and he climbed down. Manav was told to walk along the railway line. Before saying yes he asked himself what would happen if a train came round the bend, or if his foot slipped between the tracks. The answers were so clear that he did not need to argue. Dev was called a scaredy-cat, so he climbed the big tree beside the pond to prove otherwise. He ended up stuck on a branch, scraped and shaking, until an older girl helped him down. Kabir's friend fell off his bicycle during a stunt they had both joined. Kabir told his parents exactly what happened, helped his friend get home, and said quietly that next time he would say no early.

qa.q: Where did Rishi stand while the others jeered?
qa.a: Rishi stood on top of a high wall.

qa.q: How does Dev's choice differ from Manav's, and what happened to each?
qa.a: Dev accepted the dare to avoid being called scared and ended up stuck and scraped. Manav asked what could go wrong on the railway line, saw the danger and refused.

qa.q: What was Dev feeling while he sat stuck on the branch?
qa.a: Dev was probably frightened and embarrassed, since the dare he took to prove himself left him shaking and needing help.

qa.q: What could Dev say the next time someone dares him?
qa.a: He could say plainly that he does not want to, or suggest a safer game, and walk away if they keep pushing. Telling a trusted adult about the dare would also help. 🙂

grounding: Four boys meet risky dares by weighing danger against teasing, predicting what could go wrong, accepting to prove courage, and regretting a stunt afterwards.

passage: In the hospital corridor, four families were absorbing the same kind of news about a parent. Mridul asked the treating specialist to walk him through the phases, the options and what nobody could yet say. He took notes and did not act on what he had seen in videos online. Ankita and her siblings shared out the work: one handled the hospital visits, one dealt with forms and insurance, and one kept the relatives informed. A group chat and a call each week kept them together. Jahnavi's relatives arrived with costly cures that had no proof behind them. Wanting to do something, she spent her savings on several of them, and money and strength drained from her household with nobody's medical guidance. Tarun's family began a first treatment that brought hard side effects. They went back to the doctor to discuss changes, rearranged shifts at the office and in the house, and adjusted their spending rather than holding on to the opening plan.

qa.q: What did Mridul ask the specialist to explain?
qa.a: He asked the specialist to walk him through the phases, the options and what nobody could yet say.

qa.q: How does Jahnavi's approach differ from Mridul's, and what happened in each family?
qa.a: Jahnavi spent savings on unproven cures pushed by relatives, and the family's money and energy drained away. Mridul asked the specialist and took notes, so decisions rested on medical explanation.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi probably feeling when she bought the remedies?
qa.a: She was anxious and wanted to do something helpful, so she grabbed each suggestion.

qa.q: What could Jahnavi do now that her savings have gone?
qa.a: She could stop buying remedies and go back to the doctor with questions, and share the load with her family. Talking with a counsellor at the hospital about her worry might help. 🤍

grounding: Four families handle a parent's serious diagnosis by asking doctors, dividing tasks, buying unproven remedies, and revising the plan after side effects.

passage: At the final-year project fair, four teams told how they had worked. Ganga's team of four cut the project into modules, pinned each job to a common board, with an owner and a date, and met briefly twice a week to review it. Aparna's group saw that the data pipeline had to exist before the model could be trained, while the interface could be built at the same time. So they gave the pipeline's owner extra help first. Ira's team was sure the project was easy. They put off coding till the last four weeks, then hit integration bugs and rushed out a barely working submission. Kunal's team missed a milestone twice. They asked why, again and again, and found that vague requirements, and not idleness, were the cause. They wrote a single-page specification and agreed what would count as done.

qa.q: How often did Ganga's team meet to review the board?
qa.a: They met twice a week.

qa.q: How does Ira's team's timing differ from Ganga's team's, and what did each end up with?
qa.a: Ira's team postponed coding to the final month and rushed a barely working project. Ganga's team spread jobs across modules with owners and dates, and reviewed them often.

qa.q: What might Ira's team be feeling as they scramble in the last month?
qa.a: They are probably stressed and regretful, because their confidence that the project was easy proved wrong.

qa.q: What could Ira's team try for the next big task?
qa.a: They could split the work into small pieces early, put dates on each and check progress every few days. Starting the hard parts first would show problems sooner. 🙂

grounding: Four final-year teams manage a project by splitting tasks, ordering dependencies, leaving it to the last month, and finding the root cause of a missed milestone.

passage: Four students were failing a subject, and each tackled it differently. Amandeep, failing Maths, asked why over and over and traced the trail back to his shaky fractions and basic algebra from Class 8. The trouble was foundations, not the current chapter. Irawati stayed after class, showed the teacher her last three test papers, and agreed on two doubt sessions a week, which suited her better and cost less than joining a full extra batch. Sumit revised English and Biology since those felt pleasant. His marks in those rose a little, but Maths, skipped again, went on dragging his result down. Meera spent a month reading her notes again and again. Her scores hardly moved. She admitted that reading was not working, and switched to answering questions with the book closed, which showed her real weak spots within days.

qa.q: How many test papers did Irawati show her teacher?
qa.a: She showed her last three test papers.

qa.q: How does Sumit's choice of subjects differ from Amandeep's approach, and what happened to each?
qa.a: Sumit kept revising the subjects he liked and skipped Maths, so his result still dropped. Amandeep asked why and found weak basics from Class 8, so he knew what to fix.

qa.q: What might Sumit be feeling when he picks up English instead of Maths?
qa.a: He is probably avoiding discomfort and wants the good feeling of doing well, so Maths feels too hard to face.

qa.q: What could Sumit try instead?
qa.a: He could begin with ten minutes of Maths, ask a teacher what to study first, and slowly increase the time. Starting with the easiest topic may help him face the hard ones. 🙂

grounding: Students fix a failing subject by tracing the root, asking the teacher, avoiding it, and changing the method when no improvement shows.

passage: Four software teams each found their own way with AI tools. Bhavna, a team lead, wrote a short list. Writing first versions of tests and condensing published documents were fine, while pasting customer data or company secrets into open tools was not. Sachin's team tried the tools for a month, but only on documentation and drafts of unit tests. They measured how much time was saved and how many errors crept in, and only afterwards thought about using them on important code. A junior developer on another team merged code written by AI without reading it. It held an insecure query that passed the basic tests and reached the live system before a reviewer spotted it. Sangeeta's team once found a wrong figure in an AI-written report. They traced how it slipped past review, added a check step, changed their rules, and began regarding the tool as a coworker who can be mistaken.

qa.q: What did Sachin's team measure during their month of trying the tools?
qa.a: They measured how much time was saved and how many errors crept in.

qa.q: How does the junior developer's handling of AI code differ from Sangeeta's team's handling of the wrong figure, and what changed?
qa.a: The junior merged code unread, so an insecure query reached the live system. Sangeeta's team traced how the error passed review and added a check step, so the process improved.

qa.q: What might the junior developer be feeling after the reviewer finds the insecure query?
qa.a: They are probably embarrassed and worried, having trusted the tool without checking.

qa.q: What could the junior developer do from now on?
qa.a: They could read and test every piece of AI-written code, and ask a reviewer to look at anything unfamiliar before it merges. 🙂

grounding: Four teams work with AI tools by setting limits, piloting on low-risk tasks, trusting output without review, and reviewing an incident.

passage: Four founders each met public criticism online in a different way. When a harsh post about his product appeared, Siddharth waited a whole day, knowing an angry reply typed in a rage tends to make things worse and to spread the post further. Gargi's company had a complaint from one customer about a specific order. The company offered a one-to-one phone call or a personal email to sort out the details, and later came back to say it was settled, keeping the customer's privacy and staying out of a public row. Yash argued point by point with his critics and attacked their motives. Screenshots went around, and the quarrel drew much more notice than the original complaint. Amit found some posts making false and damaging claims about his firm. He gathered screenshots and consulted a lawyer on what the law allowed, but did not threaten people who simply disagreed with him.

qa.q: How long did Siddharth wait before replying?
qa.a: Siddharth waited a whole day.

qa.q: How does Yash's response to critics differ from Gargi's, and what happened in each case?
qa.a: Yash argued in public and attacked motives, so screenshots spread and the quarrel got more attention. Gargi's company moved the details to a private call or email and reported the matter settled, protecting privacy.

qa.q: What was Yash probably feeling while he argued with critics?
qa.a: He was probably angry and defensive, hurt that his work was being criticised.

qa.q: What could Yash do next to calm the situation?
qa.a: He could stop replying publicly, thank people for real feedback, and offer private contact for those with specific issues. Waiting a day before replying might help too. 🙂

grounding: Four founders meet online criticism by pausing, moving to private channels, arguing publicly, and using legal remedies only for false and harmful claims.
